AEMC: Mid-sized US companies across technology, industrials, financials and health care, picked as a core middle-tier holding. It is actively managed exposure to the market's middle: mid-caps offer more growth room than giants, and the near-even spread across sectors keeps any one industry from dominating.
AEMG: Mid-sized growth companies, led by technology at about 40%, with industrials, health care and consumer stocks behind it. It is an actively managed growth holding in the market's middle tier: mid-cap growers can compound faster than giants, but they also swing more.
AEMV: Mid-sized companies trading at value prices, spread fairly evenly across financials, health care, industrials and technology. It is an actively managed value holding in the market's middle tier: the even sector spread keeps it balanced, and it tends to lag when growth stocks lead.
AESB: Small companies across financials, health care, technology and industrials, picked as a core small-cap holding. It is actively managed exposure to the market's smallest tier: small companies offer the most growth room and diversification across sectors, with bigger swings than large stocks.
AESG: Small growth companies, with health care the biggest slice at about a quarter, followed by technology, financials and industrials. It is an actively managed growth bet on smaller firms: they have the most room to grow, and the widest swings to go with it.
AESL: Small companies trading at value prices, led by financials at over a quarter, with real estate, industrials and health care behind it. It is an actively managed bargain hunt in the market's smallest tier: value small-caps can be overlooked gems, but they can also stay cheap for years.
AICH: Chinese companies building artificial intelligence, from chip and software firms to the platforms applying AI, mostly technology with some industrials. It is a single-country AI bet: it concentrates on China's tech race, so trade tensions and Chinese regulation hit it directly.
AIMG: Ten publicly traded companies at the center of the artificial intelligence value chain, from chips and cloud platforms to the software built on them. It is a concentrated AI bet: only ten names carry the whole fund, so it swings hard with the AI trade.
ARKT: The ARK Innovation ETF wrapped in a buffer for a twelve-month outcome period starting in the fourth quarter, softening part of any loss in that volatile growth fund while capping gains. The defense is the point: it trades some upside for a cushion under a fund famous for big swings.
AZYY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged Amazon fund, which doubles the stock's daily moves before the options even come into play. It is an aggressive income trade: leverage plus options means fast swings, and it is built for short holding periods, not steady saving.
BPH: One company, BP, held through its US-listed depositary receipts with a built-in hedge that removes most of the pound-to-dollar exchange rate effect. It is a single-stock energy bet with the currency risk stripped out, so the result follows BP's business alone.
BSTU: US Treasury bonds that all mature around 2030, held in a single fund that winds down as that year arrives. It is a goal-based income holding: the shared maturity date makes its interest-rate sensitivity predictable, and prices fall if rates rise before 2030.
BTCK: A fixed mix of 80% bitcoin and 20% carbon credit futures, blending a crypto asset with contracts tied to the price of pollution permits. It is an unusual diversifier: the carbon slice is meant to move differently from bitcoin, though both parts can be volatile.
CLOD: Cloud computing companies in developed markets: the software, hosting and platform firms that rent computing power and tools over the internet. It is a focused technology bet: cloud names dominate, so it swings with tech spending and leaves out most other industries.
CRIB: Real estate companies from around the world, including the United States: property owners, developers and REITs across many countries. It is a global property holding for income and diversification, with currency swings and foreign housing markets added to the usual real estate risks.
CTWO: European Union carbon allowances, the permits that factories and power plants must hold to emit carbon under the EU cap-and-trade system. It is a pure bet on carbon prices: the fund owns the allowances themselves, so it rises and falls with EU climate policy and energy markets.
DEPW: Companies in the ecosystem around Google's DeepMind AI lab: technology names, the utilities powering data centers, and media and finance firms touched by its research. It is a focused AI bet built around one lab's orbit, so it captures partners and suppliers, not just one stock.
DICE: Companies that run trading platforms and prediction markets, mostly financial firms plus the technology providers behind them. It is a focused bet on betting and trading going mainstream: the theme is narrow and policy-sensitive, since gambling and event contracts draw regulatory attention.
EAFG: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, screened for strong free cash flow margins, led by technology and consumer stocks. It is a growth holding with a cash-generation filter: the screen favors profitable self-funding companies over flashier growers.
EGLE: S&P 500 companies that earn at least half their revenue inside the United States, so the fund leans toward domestic businesses across technology, financials and health care. It is a core holding with a homegrown tilt: multinational exporters weigh less here than in the plain index.
ESBG: Three asset classes in one fund, US large-cap stocks, intermediate Treasury bonds and gold, reached through futures on top of a Treasury base. It is a balanced diversifier: the gold and bonds are there to soften stock drops, though futures keep the mix more complex than it looks.
FGSI: US stocks screened for growth strength, paired with sold call options on the S&P 500 to add a target level of income. It mixes growth and payouts: the options generate regular income but trim how much the fund gains when the market runs.
FRUT: A short named list of giant growth companies, the MANGOS group of mega-cap technology and tech-adjacent names, held through their stocks. It is a concentrated bet on a handful of market leaders: there is no diversification cushion, so it swings hard with those few names.
GOIB: Income built around a single stock, Alphabet, Google's parent, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost payouts from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet: the income strategy rides on one company's stock, so its swings set the fund's fate.
KCHP: South Korean semiconductor companies, the chipmakers and equipment firms behind memory and processor production. It is a single-country, single-industry bet: it rides the global chip cycle and the Korean market at once, so currency and export swings both matter.
KEO: Equity income built from Kurv's own option income funds and direct stock and option positions, aiming for regular payouts from share prices. It is a fund-of-funds income strategy: the payouts come from option premiums across several holdings, and gains are capped wherever the underlying funds cap theirs.
KRYP: The 20 largest and most traded crypto assets, reached through futures and other financial instruments rather than by holding coins directly. It is a broad crypto basket in one fund: bitcoin and its biggest rivals move it most, and futures pricing can drift from spot prices.
LFBE: US Treasury securities arranged to pay out a planned stream of income through the year 2065, the longest horizon in its family of income funds. It is built for lifelong income planning: the payments are the product, set on a schedule that runs for decades.
LIFT: US Treasury securities arranged to pay out a planned stream of income ending in 2028, with the schedule set in advance. It is an income planning tool for a near horizon: the fixed end date makes payouts predictable, and it behaves more like a maturing bond than a regular fund.
LQAI: Large US stocks chosen with help from artificial intelligence models that scan company data for likely winners, led by technology at a bit over a third. It is a core equity holding with a machine doing the analysis: the AI tilt sets it apart, but it still moves with the market.
PCR: Private credit exposures, meaning loans to companies made outside the banking system, reached through index-linked instruments rather than direct lending. It is an income holding with less transparency than regular bonds: the loans are hard to value daily, and losses land when borrowers struggle.
PLYY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged Palantir fund, stacking options on top of a fund that already amplifies the stock's daily moves. It is an aggressive short-term income trade: the double leverage makes swings extreme, so it suits active traders, not steady savers.
PQV: Large US stocks through options on the S&P 500, with a built-in cushion that absorbs the first 5% of losses over each quarterly outcome period. It suits cautious investors: the smaller buffer means a higher cap on gains than deeper-protection funds, and terms reset every three months.
PSAI: The 100 S&P 500 companies with the strongest artificial intelligence exposure, chosen by an AI-driven scoring approach across all industries. It is a concentrated growth bet on the AI leaders among big US companies, so it swings more than the full index.
QBY: Weekly income from selling put options on a leveraged fund tied to D-Wave Quantum, a quantum computing company. It stacks options on leverage on one speculative stock, so payouts can be large but swings are extreme and it is built for short holding periods.
QFRD: S&P 500 companies that combine strong free cash flow with heavy research spending, which tilts the fund heavily to technology at about two thirds, plus health care. It is a growth holding with an innovation filter: it favors firms that fund their own future, and swings with tech.
QMID: Mid-sized US companies screened for both quality and growth, spread across technology, health care, industrials and consumer stocks. It is a growth holding in the market's middle tier: the quality screen aims for sturdier growers, but mid-caps still swing more than large companies.
QQMY: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May. It blends tech growth with defense: gains are capped, and the May start date fixes the protection terms.
SCA: An autocallable note tied to a single stock, Super Micro Computer, a structured contract that pays income and can end early if the stock behaves. It is concentrated income with fine print: everything rides on one volatile AI hardware stock, and losses arrive if it falls far enough.
SFYI: The 50 most widely followed stocks on social media and brokerage platforms, paired with options to generate income from them. It is a popularity contest turned into a portfolio: holdings follow retail investor buzz, so the mix can chase whatever is trending.
SHPP: Industrial and logistics companies from around the world: airlines, shipping, trucking, rail and warehouse operators that keep goods moving. It is a focused bet on global trade and transport, so it rises and falls with shipping volumes and the world economy.
SJLD: Short-term investment-grade bonds and some preferred shares, actively managed to keep the portfolio's average maturity under two years. It is a low-drama income holding: the short maturities mean its price barely moves when interest rates change, though payouts stay modest.
SOLM: Exposure to Solana's SOL token through regulated Solana funds, combined with selling options on them to generate monthly income. It pairs a volatile crypto asset with an income overlay: option premiums add payouts, but capped gains mean it trails a straight SOL rally.
STHH: One company, STMicroelectronics, the European chipmaker, held through its US-listed depositary receipts with a built-in hedge against euro moves. It is a single-stock technology bet with currency swings removed, so the result follows the chip business alone, for better or worse.
TDOG: A single crypto asset, Dogecoin, the meme-born token, held directly by the trust. It is a pure price bet on one of the most sentiment-driven coins: there is no income and no diversification, and the price can swing wildly on social media mood.
TIPE: A ladder of inflation-linked bonds arranged to pay out income through 2031, with payments that adjust as consumer prices rise. It is an income planning tool with built-in inflation protection: the 2031 end date fixes the schedule, and the payouts rise with inflation instead of losing ground to it.
TIPF: A ladder of inflation-linked bonds arranged to pay out income through 2036, with payments that adjust as consumer prices rise. It is a longer-horizon income planning tool: the inflation link protects purchasing power, and the fixed 2036 schedule makes the payout path predictable.
TIPH: A ladder of inflation-linked bonds arranged to pay out income through 2056, with payments that adjust as consumer prices rise. It is built for very long income horizons: the decades-long schedule sets it apart, and the inflation link keeps payouts from losing purchasing power over time.
TSIB: Income built around a single stock, Tesla, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost payouts from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet on one famously volatile company: the income plan cannot tame Tesla's swings, it only harvests them.
XSPC: Companies building the space economy and the AI that supports it: launch, satellites and orbital infrastructure, split between industrials and technology. It is a speculative growth bet on two hot themes at once, so it can swing hard when either theme cools.
